title: Pip and the Red Ball
text: Pip the puppy found a red ball in the yard. He pushed it with his nose. The ball rolled under a bench. Mia reached under the bench and gave it back. Pip wagged his tail.

questions.why: The first sentence says Pip found a red ball.
The ball rolled under a bench.
Mia reached under the bench.

questions.q: How did Pip push the ball?
questions.why: The story says he pushed it with his nose.

questions.q: What did Pip do at the end?
questions.why: The last sentence says Pip wagged his tail.

title: The Tiny Seed
text: Nora planted a seed in a small pot. She put the pot by the window. Every day, she gave it a little water. One morning, a green sprout popped up. Nora smiled.

questions.why: Nora planted a seed.

questions.q: Where did she put the pot?
questions.why: She put it by the window.

questions.q: What did Nora give the seed?
questions.why: She watered it every day.
A green sprout popped up.
Nora smiled when she saw the sprout.

title: A Rainy Walk
text: Owen looked outside and saw rain. He put on his yellow boots and blue coat. He took an umbrella to the bus stop. A big puddle was by the curb. Owen walked around it.

questions.why: Owen saw rain outside.
The boots were yellow.
He took an umbrella to the bus stop.
The story mentions a big puddle.

questions.q: What did Owen do about the puddle?
questions.why: Owen walked around the puddle.

title: The Lost Mittens
text: It was a cold day. Ava had two pink mittens. She took them off to build a snowman. Later, she could find only one mitten. Her brother Leo saw the other mitten near a tree. He brought it to Ava.

questions.why: She could find only one mitten.
They were pink mittens.
Ava built a snowman.
Her brother Leo saw it.
Leo saw it near a tree.

title: The Library Surprise
text: Ella wanted a book about whales. At the library, she first looked on the animal shelf. She could not find it, so she asked Ms. Kim for help. Ms. Kim showed her a new shelf of ocean books. Ella borrowed a whale book and read it with Dad that night.

questions.q: What kind of book did Ella want?
questions.why: She wanted a whale book.
She first checked the animal shelf.

questions.q: Why did Ella ask Ms. Kim for help?
options: She could not find the book
questions.why: She could not find what she wanted.

questions.q: What did Ms. Kim show her?
questions.why: Ms. Kim showed her the ocean books.
That night she read with Dad.

title: The Picnic Plan
text: Theo and his sister planned a picnic. In the morning, they made cheese sandwiches and filled a bottle with water. At noon, they carried their basket to the park. Dark clouds gathered, so they sat under the picnic shelter. When the rain stopped, they played tag.

questions.q: What did they make to eat?
questions.why: They made cheese sandwiches.

questions.q: When did they go to the park?
questions.why: They went at noon.

questions.q: Why did they sit under the shelter?
questions.why: The shelter helped when it rained.

questions.q: What did they do after the rain?
questions.why: They played tag when the rain stopped.
They prepared food before leaving.

title: The Blue Birdhouse
text: Ben and Grandpa made a birdhouse from wood. Ben painted it blue while Grandpa fixed the roof. They hung it on an old apple tree. For three days, no birds came. On the fourth morning, a little bird landed on the roof. Ben was excited but stayed quiet so he would not scare it.

questions.q: What did Ben and Grandpa build?
questions.why: They built a birdhouse.
Ben painted it blue.
They hung it on an apple tree.

questions.q: When did a bird finally come?
questions.why: The bird landed on the fourth morning.

options: He did not want to scare the bird
questions.why: Staying quiet would keep the bird calm.

title: The Missing Lunchbox
text: Jules put a green lunchbox beside his backpack before school. At lunchtime, it was missing. He checked his desk and the coat hooks. Then he remembered that he had visited the art room that morning. His lunchbox was on a table there. He thanked the teacher and returned to class.

questions.why: It was green.

questions.q: When did Jules notice it was missing?
questions.why: He noticed at lunchtime.

questions.q: Where did he look before the art room?
questions.why: He checked his desk and the coat hooks.
It was on a table in the art room.
He remembered being in the art room.

title: The Bridge of Stones
text: Maya and Sol walked beside a narrow stream. The wooden footbridge was closed for repairs. They noticed a row of large flat stones across the shallow water. Sol wanted to jump across, but Maya suggested they use the marked trail to a second bridge. The trail took longer, yet their shoes stayed dry and they crossed safely.

questions.q: Why was the first bridge unavailable?
questions.why: The bridge was closed for repairs.

questions.q: What did Sol first want to do?
questions.why: Sol wanted to jump across.
They crossed on a marked route instead of jumping.

questions.q: What does “yet” signal in the last sentence?
questions.why: The path took longer, but they stayed safe.
Maya considered safety before speed.

title: A Light in the Window
text: Each evening, Mr. Chen placed a lamp in his front window. A new neighbor, Amira, wondered why. One foggy evening, she saw a mail carrier use the warm light to find the right house. The next day, Amira asked Mr. Chen about the lamp. He explained that his street had few bright signs, so the lamp helped visitors find their way.

questions.q: When did Mr. Chen put out the lamp?
questions.why: He placed it in the window each evening.
Amira wondered why the lamp was there.

questions.q: Who used the light during the fog?
questions.why: A mail carrier used the light.

options: The street had few bright signs
questions.why: Visitors needed an easy way to find the house.

questions.q: What can you infer about Mr. Chen?
questions.why: He keeps the lamp on to help people.

title: The Garden Contest
text: Two classes entered a school garden contest. Class A planted many flowers close together. Class B left spaces between their seedlings and added compost. A month later, some of Class A’s plants looked weak, while Class B had sturdy stems and bright leaves. The classes discussed their methods and decided to share ideas before next year’s contest.

questions.why: They entered a school garden contest.

questions.q: How did Class B plant differently?
questions.why: Class B left spaces and added compost.
Class B had sturdy stems and bright leaves.

questions.q: Why might space between plants help?
questions.why: Plants compete less for space and resources.

questions.q: What did the students decide to do next?
questions.why: The classes decided to share ideas.

title: The Noisy Attic
text: At bedtime, Rowan heard tapping above his room. He imagined a giant bird on the roof. The next day, he told Aunt May, who brought a flashlight and climbed the attic stairs. They found a loose window latch moving in the wind. Aunt May fastened the latch, and that night the tapping stopped. Rowan laughed at his earlier guess.

questions.why: He heard tapping above his room.
He imagined a giant bird.
The latch moved in the wind.
Fixing the latch stopped the sound.
The real cause was different from Rowan’s guess.

title: The Midnight Telescope
text: On Saturday, Celia visited the science club to watch a meteor shower. At first, clouds covered the sky, and several children wanted to leave. Their guide explained that meteor showers are easier to see after the sky clears and our eyes adjust to darkness. The group waited quietly, turned off their flashlights, and told stories. Soon the clouds drifted away. Celia spotted a bright streak and understood why patience mattered.

questions.q: What was the group hoping to see?
questions.why: They came to watch a meteor shower.

questions.q: Why did some children want to leave?
questions.why: The sky was cloudy at first.

questions.q: Why did they turn off their flashlights?
options: To help their eyes adjust to darkness
To save batteries for a game
questions.why: Dark adaptation can help people see faint lights.
After waiting, the sky cleared.

questions.q: What is a main theme of the story?
questions.why: Celia learned the value of waiting.

title: The Map in the Bottle
text: During a beach cleanup, Hana discovered a sealed bottle caught in seaweed. Inside was a hand-drawn map of the nearby dunes. She hoped it led to treasure, but a note beside the map read, “Follow the marked path to protect nesting birds.” Hana brought it to a park ranger. The ranger explained that volunteers had created the map years earlier to show visitors a safe route. Hana felt proud that her discovery might help protect wildlife.

questions.q: Where did Hana find the bottle?
questions.why: It was caught in seaweed during cleanup.

questions.q: What did Hana first hope the map showed?
questions.why: She hoped the map led to treasure.

questions.q: What was the map really for?
questions.why: It showed a safe route to avoid the birds.

questions.q: Why did Hana bring it to a ranger?
questions.why: A ranger could explain the map.

options: From treasure hunting to protecting wildlife
From liking birds to hating birds
From being afraid of sand to water
From loving maps to hating them
questions.why: She discovers a different, meaningful kind of treasure.

title: The Team with No Captain
text: At recess, a group of children wanted to organize a basketball game. Everyone argued about who should be captain, and the clock kept ticking. Priya suggested rotating the role each time they played. That way, every player could lead and everyone could spend more time playing. The group agreed. They finished two games before the bell, and even the quietest player volunteered to be captain next time.

questions.q: What stopped the game from starting?
options: An argument over who would lead
questions.why: The children argued about the captain.
She suggested rotating the role.

options: Everyone got a chance to lead
It made the bell ring later
questions.why: Rotation made the role fair.

questions.q: What detail shows the team became more confident?
options: A quiet player volunteered next time
questions.why: The quietest player volunteered.
Sharing leadership got the game moving.

title: The River After Rain
text: After heavy rain, a local stream turned brown and rushed faster than usual. Devon planned to photograph otters on the opposite bank, but the usual stepping stones were underwater. His friend Lila reminded him that fast water can hide deep spots. Instead of crossing, they stayed on the safe trail and used binoculars. They still captured several wonderful photos, including one of an otter carrying a fish.

options: The stream became faster and muddy
questions.why: The stream turned brown and rushed faster.

questions.q: Why were the stepping stones unusable?
options: They were on the other bank
questions.why: The stones were covered by water.

options: Fast water may hide deep places
questions.why: She warned about unseen deep spots.

questions.q: How did they still get photos?
options: They watched from a safe trail
questions.why: They used binoculars and stayed safe.

options: The friends chose safety and still succeeded
The friends gave up all hope
questions.why: Safety did not stop them from enjoying wildlife.

title: The Clockmaker’s Promise
text: For decades, Mr. Vale repaired the clock in the town square. When he became ill, the clock stopped, and people began arriving late to meetings. A young apprentice named Iris offered to help. She studied the gears and found one worn wheel, but the replacement would take a week to arrive. Instead of pretending she could fix everything at once, Iris posted a clear notice explaining the delay. Neighbors began carrying small watches and helping visitors find their way. When the wheel arrived, Iris repaired the clock with Mr. Vale watching proudly. The town had learned to solve problems together.

questions.q: What first caused a problem in town?
questions.why: The stopped clock led people to arrive late.
She found a worn wheel inside the clock.

questions.q: Why did Iris post a notice?
options: To explain the repair delay honestly
questions.why: The new wheel would take time to arrive.

questions.q: What does the neighbors’ response show?
options: People can cooperate during a setback
questions.why: They helped one another while waiting.
Iris explained the issue and the community worked together.

title: The Hidden Meadow
text: During a nature walk, Soren noticed bright butterflies gathering near a patch of wildflowers. His friend Wren wanted to pick a bouquet to take home. Their guide pointed out that the flowers provided food for butterflies and bees, and that many insects relied on the meadow throughout the summer. Wren decided to sketch the flowers instead. Later, the friends showed their drawings at school and suggested planting native flowers in an empty courtyard. Soon other classmates volunteered to help. A small choice in the meadow had grown into a project for the whole school.

questions.q: Why were butterflies near the meadow?
questions.why: The guide says the flowers feed insects.

questions.q: What did Wren decide to do instead of picking flowers?
questions.why: Wren chose to sketch them.
The friends shared what they had learned.

questions.q: What does “A small choice ... had grown” mean?
options: One thoughtful action inspired a bigger change
questions.why: A personal choice inspired classmates.

questions.q: Which evidence best supports caring for habitats?
options: Many insects rely on flowers for food
questions.why: Food for insects is the key reason not to pick them.

title: The Last Piece of the Puzzle
text: A family spent the weekend assembling a thousand-piece puzzle of a snowy mountain. On Sunday evening, the last piece was missing. Tessa blamed her brother for losing it, although she had not seen him touch the puzzle. Her brother quietly searched beneath the table and found nothing. Later, Tessa noticed the missing piece stuck inside the folded puzzle box. She apologized for making an unfair guess. Her brother accepted the apology, and they placed the final piece together. Tessa realized that being certain is not the same as having proof.

questions.why: They worked on a thousand-piece puzzle.

options: She had no evidence her brother lost it
Her brother was away all weekend
questions.why: She had not seen him touch the missing piece.
Tessa found it in the box.

questions.q: How did Tessa repair the situation?
questions.why: She said sorry for the unfair guess.

options: Look for evidence before blaming someone
A missing item is always stolen
questions.why: Being sure does not mean having proof.

title: A Message Across the Bay
text: The sailing club planned a race across a quiet bay. Just before the start, the wind shifted and thick fog rolled in. Some sailors argued that delaying the race would disappoint the crowd. Coach Ana explained that the markers on the far shore were difficult to see and that boats might stray into deeper shipping lanes. She postponed the start and invited everyone to study weather maps together. By afternoon, the fog lifted, but the club still shortened the route. The racers finished safely, and several young sailors said they had learned more from the decision than from the race itself.

questions.q: What changed right before the race?
questions.why: The weather changed unexpectedly.

questions.q: Why did some people oppose delaying?
options: They worried the crowd would be disappointed
questions.why: They feared upsetting the crowd.

questions.q: What specific risk did Coach Ana identify?
questions.why: Fog hid markers and could send boats off course.

questions.q: Why did they shorten the route even after fog lifted?
questions.why: They adjusted the race for safety.

options: Good leaders put safety ahead of pressure
questions.why: Ana resisted pressure and made an informed choice.
